Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, members of the Committee on Labor, l'm Beth White, Director of Politics and Legislation for the Maine Service Employees Association, Local 1989 of the
Service Employees International Union. We are a labor union representing over 13,000 Maine
workers, including retirees from all three branches of Maine State Government.
First, on behalf of all the members of MSEA-SElU Local 1989, we thank you for the work you are
doing to try to undo the 2011 pension cuts. We appreciate the bipartisan work this Committee has
done to help advocate for improvements to our retiree pensions and to understand the challenges
presented by the Unfunded Actuarial Liability (UAL). However, since there is much more work to be done to correct the wrongs of the 2011 cuts, we're here today in support of three pieces of
legislation related to pensions:
0 LD 1040, An Act to Raise the Cap on Retirement Benefits for Certain State Employees and Teachers to Which a Cost-of-living Adjustment is Made, sponsored by Rep. Dodge
0 LD 900, An Act to Protect State Retiree Pensions from Inflation, sponsored by Sen. Baldacci 0 LD 1003, An Act Establishing the Retirement Benefit lmprovement Fund, sponsored by Rep
Dodge LD 1003 is a creative solution to ensure there are funds being set aside to be used for pension
improvements, especially as we approach 2028 when the UAL will be paid down and we will have the opportunity to fully undo the 2011 cuts without triggering such large fiscal notes. While we
support LD 1040 and hope to see it passed and funded, it's important to note that this would only make changes for retirees who retired before the 2011 cuts occurred; while this is certainly a step in the right direction and a way to make improvements without triggering such a large fiscal note, we want to flag for the Committee that we will continue to fight in future sessions to undo the cuts
for all retirees, regardless of retirement date.
As you may know, ever since 2011, when MainePERS pensions were cut to fund tax cuts for the wealthy, many retired state employees and teachers have struggled to keep up with the cost of
living. The 2011 cuts included a freeze on retirees' cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) for 2011,
2012, and 2013; a 3% cap on all future cost-of-living adjustments; and a permanent limit on cost-of-
living adjustments so they only apply to the first $20,000 of pension income, adjusted for inflation.
There is widespread, bipartisan recognition that the 2011 pension cuts went too far. Solutions have
been offered by Democrat and Republican legislators, and we appreciate the progress that has been made. However, it's important to remember that Maine's retired state workers and teachers still have not fully recovered what they lost to the 2011 cuts. Several of our members will testify today to explain how they have been directly impacted by the drastic reductions in cost-of-living adjustments over the past 14 years. Bill Brown, Director of Actuarial and Legislative Affairs
LD 1003, An Act Establishing the Retirement Benefit Improvement Fund

Good morning, Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder and other distinguished members of
the Joint Standing Committee on Labor. I am Bill Brown, Director of Actuarial and Legislative
Affairs for the Maine Public Employees Retirement System (MainePERS).

MainePERS is neither for nor against LD 1003. We are here to provide information and to offer
any assistance the committee may request regarding this bill.

State employee and teacher retirement benefits are subject to cost of living adjustments
(COLAs) tied to the Consumer Price Index (CPI). The current cap on COLA is 3%, established in 2011. Also in 2011 the amount of a retiree's benefit to which the COLA applies ("COLA Base") was limited to $20,000, indexed annually based on the percentage of COLA paid. The 2025 COLA base is $26,428.98. A sheet detailing the most recent history of COLA changes is
attached to this testimony.
As proposed, Section 2 of LD 1003 establishes a non-lapsing fund in Part 20 of Title 5 to accumulate a portion of year-end unappropriated General Fund surpluses for the purpose of
increasing the COLA Base. When it is determined that the fund contains sufficient funds to increase the COLA Base by at least $500, the State Controller would transfer the funds
necessary to do so to MainePERS.

This committee is well aware that changes to the COLA Base require significant upfront funding
since the Maine Constitution does not permit the creation of new or- additional benefits unless
they are immediately and full funded. However, there is no fiscal impact associated with this bill
as drafted as it does not make any appropriation to create any new benefits. Rather, LD 1003
proposes to establish a fund in which to set aside funding as described in the bill to gradually
increase and/or eliminate the COLA Base over time.

The fund as proposed in the bill appears consistent with other funds that are held and administered
by the State of Maine. If it is the intent of the bill for the fund to be administered by the State of
Maine, we would suggest the State Controller be responsible for the annual report on the status of the fund. If, however, it is the intent of the bill that the fund be administered by MainePERS we are
available to work with the bill sponsor and the committee analyst on the language. -

Thank you for your consideration of this testimony. I am happy to take your questions and be
present for the work session.

Testimony of Rep. Jan Dodge introducing
LD 1003, An Act Establishing the Retirement Benefit Improvement Fund
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Labor

Good morning, Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder and esteemed colleagues of the Labor Committee. My
name is Jan Dodge, and I represent House District #3 9-Belfast, Northpoit and Belmont. I am here today to introduce LD I003, An Act Establishing the Retirement Benefit Improvement Fund.
About fourteen years ago a state budget was brought into balance by changing retirement rules and statutes which resulted in reduced benefits promised to retired state workers and retired teachers.
These adjustments to retirement age, reduced Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) percentage, a cap on the
amount to which the COLA is applied, threatening actions of "Retire now or you will not be eligible for health
insurance," and the mischaracterization of the level of benefits offered and paid for as shown by the recent
proposed correction to Medicare Part B and the wait of over a decade for an increase in the percentage of health
insurance paid to retired teachers in the state summarizes the collective harm retirees have endured for a decade and a half! This also represents the bills I have introduced, cosponsored and supported over the past six years.
This bill seeks to put retirees in line for an amount of money from the Cascade to be added to the base amount
to which the COLA is applied. It will go into effect when enough money is available to increase this amount in
$500 increments.
The language was drafted to mimic the places funds would go first that are already in statute -- lines 31-39 on page one (1) and lines 4-12 on page two (2).
I am bringing this bill forward because the Chief Executive suggested I, and my legislative colleagues
concerned with these issues, develop multiple creative approaches to correct the resulting deficits from the previous Chief Executive and lack of corrective actions by several legislatures. Special thanks to Rachel Tremblay in the Office of Fiscal and Program Review (OFPR), policy staff, bill cosponsors, especially Reps.
Boyer, Macias and McCabe who I hope will take up this mantle after my time in the legislature has ended!
Please support LD 1003. It adds a tool to the toolbox to correct injustices and unkept promises suffered by
retired state workers and retired teachers in Maine.
Thank you.

District 39: Belfast, Belmont & Northport

TESTIMONY OF THOMAS RECORD MAINE ASSOCIATION OF RETIREES
IN SUPPORT OF
LD 1003, AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE REIREMENT BENEFIT V IMPROVEMENT FUND
PRESENTED TO THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON LABOR
MARCH 26, 2025
Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, Members of the Committee, l am Thomas Record and l
testify today on behalf of the Maine Association of Retiree (MAR) in support of LD 1003.
We would like to thank Representative Dodge and the cosponsors for bringing forth this bill which seeks to address the issue which is the single most important issue raised to MAR by our
membership. For most retired state employees and educators, pensions through the Maine Public Employees Retirement System (MainePERS) are their main source of income. Most of these retirees do not receive social security benefits based on their public service.
Prior to 2011, MainePERS retirement benefits contained an annual cost-of-living adjustment
(COLA) which was applied to their entire MainePERS benefit subject to a maximum of 4%. ln 2011,
however, there were significant MainePERS pension cuts, including a three-year freeze on COLAs, a
reduction in the maximum COLA from 4% to 3%, and application of the COLA to only the first $20,000 of a retiree's pension? That $20,000 amount was indexed and is now $26,428,98 fourteen years later.
The obvious effect of the 2011 COLA cut has been to leave these retired state workers and educators especially vulnerable to inflation. There have been several efforts to restore, in whole or in part, the COLA provisions to its pre-2011 form. These include LD 70 in the 131" Legislature which was
unanimously supported by this Committee. MAR members are thankful for that support. The situation
is complicated, however, by Article 10, �18-A of the Maine Constitution which, in pertinent part, prohibits the creation of any unfunded liabilities for MainePERS except for those resulting for experience losses. The practical effect ofthis requirement to fully fund any benefit increases in the year of enactment is to create large fiscal notes for bills containing significant restoration of COLA benefits which in turn leads to those proposals not being enacted. For example, LD 70 in the 131" had a fiscal note of nearly $1.2 billion and is a non-starter in the appropriations process.
1 2011, PL C380, Pt T, �1O.

LD 1003 takes a different approach. lt proposes earmarking a new fund, the Retirement Benefit Improvement Fund, for the receipt of unappropriated surplus funds in any fiscal year beginning with the year ending June 30, 2026 as part of the so-called "cascade" for which unappropriated surplus is used. Funds within the Retirement Benefit Improvement Fund would be used to pay for retirement benefit
improvements for retired state employees and educators and their beneficiaries. This procedure would remain in effect until such time as the COLA is applied to member's full retirement.
We have been clown the road of bills which, although conceptually supported by many
legislators, die on the Appropriations Table for lack of funding. The creative approach set forth in LD
1003 provides a funding source for restoring MainePERS retirement benefits to those who deserve them
at least in fiscal years when there is an unappropriated surplus. For that reason, MAR supports the bill.
Thank you. I'd be happy to try to answer any questions you may have.

189004:
LD 1003 An Act of Establishing the Retirement Benefit Improvement Fund
Hello,
My name is Tony Beaumier, and I am writing to advocate for LD 1003, a needed act to
establish a retirement benefit improvement fund.
I grew up in Portland, Maine, attended the University of Maine at Farmington, and
became a teacher in York, Maine, in 1985. I have been lucky to spend the last 40 years
in the classroom teaching reading and writing to middle school students.
As I approach the end of my career, I look forward to retirement. I have always had to be frugal with my earnings as a teacher. I have three children and own my home in South Ben/vick, Maine. For the last 40 years, I have contributed to MainePERS for my retirement. I could not contribute to any other retirement plan as my teaching salary barely paid the bills of owning a home and raising my family.
Unfortunately, I did not learn until last year that Governor Lepage's administration changed the retirement benefits for teachers and other state employees in 2011. Most
teachers who I have spoken to know nothing about this. Last year, having paid off my home loan, I planned to teach for a few more years to put money aside and then retire. Now, I am very concerned about what retirement holds for me and my family. Only making a COLA on the first $25,000 of my retirement with a cap of 3% leaves me wondering ifl can stay in my home. Mostly, I am concerned that I will be a burden on my children. I am afraid after a few years, I will be unable to stay at home and pay my bills.
Every year, l will lose buying power and fall further behind. I talk to retired teachers in
their 70s who say it catches up to them. Paying for heating oil, health insurance, groceries, prescription drugs, etc., when just a few years ago, inflation crept up to 8.7%
in 2023 takes its toll.
Teachers and other state employees who have served their communities deserve to
retire and live their final years with a fair and respectful retirement pension that will enable them to live with dignity and not burden their families. However, politicians significantly reduced their pensions in 2011, risking our retirement.
Please take these first steps in making things right by supporting LD 1003.
Thank you, Tony Beaumier South Bervvick, Maine

While we appreciate and thank you for the work done during past legislative sessions to make progress on this issue, there is much more to be done. We know the cost of restoring these devastating cuts in their entirety is difficult, so we ask you to continue to be creative and work with MSEA, MAR, MEA and MainePERS.
Due to these cost-of-living cuts, the 2011 Legislature and former Governor are responsible for a growing population of retired state workers and teachers who are struggling to make ends meet, with some even losing their homes, turning to food banks, applying for heating assistance, and losing the earned financial stability that they were promised. It's past time to right the wrongs that were inflicted on these Mainers who dedicated their careers to serving our great state. They deserve to enjoy their retirement with stability, dignity and comfort after everything they have done for Maine.
Thank you and I would be happy to answer any questions.

Maine superintendents firmly believe that our state must do more for the financial well-being of our educators. Our association supports increasing pay for our current educators, and we believe Maine must do more to ensure our teachers can keep up with the cost-of-living during their retirement.
For more than a decade, benefits for Maine's retired educators have simply not kept up. Inflation has continually outpaced cost-of-living adjustments. March 26, 2025
Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and esteemed members of the Labor Committee, I am Steven Bailey, the executive director of the Maine School Boards Association, testifying on behalf of the MSBA Legislative Committee neither for nor against L.D. 1003, An Act Establishing the Retirement Benefit Improvement Fund.
Maine school board members commend the goals of this bill and feel it addresses an important issue: improving the purchasing power for retired state employees. This new fund, as described in the bill, could "increase by at least $500 the portion of the retirement benefit in which cost-of-living adjustments are applied."
This is badly needed. Our members know that educators who have retired from our school districts have not seen their pension benefits keep up with the rising cost-ofliving, and this bill proposes a commonsense solution to use available fiscal resources to slowly chip away at this longstanding challenge. We also appreciate that the fund created in L.D. 1003 would not necessarily require ongoing funds, but would allow the legislature to use leftover funding, over time, to support this initiative.
Our members' only concern with this bill is whether it should be a priority at a time when there is so much financial uncertainty. The state budget is much tighter than in previous years, and board members are deeply concerned about potential federal education cuts that could threaten school meals and extra support and programming for students in poverty.
These are serious threats that could harm our local school districts. While we think L.D. 1003 is a good idea in concept, we believe your committee, and the legislature as a whole, should prioritize other essential needs in our schools and communities.
